start: For each position, ask: what is the longest run with no repeat that ends exactly here? For `"abba"` those runs are `a`, `ab`, `b` and `ba`. The answer is the longest of them, and notice that each run starts at or after the start of the one before it.

Keep `left`, where the current run starts, and a dict from each character to the last index you saw it at. When `text[right]` was last seen at or after `left`, move `left` to one past that index; a copy from before `left` is outside the run and must not pull `left` back. Replace the best only when strictly longer, so ties keep the earliest start.

start.text: The shape, with the two decisions left to you:
start.code:
def longest_unique_window(text):
    ...  # ValueError unless text is a str
    left, last, best = 0, {}, (0, 0)
    for right, c in enumerate(text):
        if c in last and ...:  # that earlier copy is inside the run
            left = ...
        last[c] = right
        if ...:  # [left, right + 1) is strictly longer than best
            best = (left, right + 1)
    return best

test_boundaries: `"abba"` must give `(0, 2)`, `""` gives `(0, 0)`, `"aaaa"` gives `(0, 1)`, and `"🙂é🙂x"` gives `(1, 4)`: indices count code points and `end` is exclusive. `longest_unique_window([])` must raise `ValueError`; an empty list loops zero times, so without a type check it returns `(0, 0)`.

On `"abba"`, `(1, 4)` means the last `a` pulled `left` back to 1, though that earlier `a` is outside the run. `(2, 4)` means a tie replaced the first answer: replace only when strictly longer. `(0, 1)` means the end is inclusive; it should be one past the last character.
test_substring_oracle: All 1,093 strings of up to 6 letters from `abc`, against a brute force over every slice `text[i:j]`: the longest with no repeated letter, and the smallest `i` among equals. The answer is the tuple `(start, end)` with `end` exclusive, so `text[start:end]` is the run itself.

The failure shows the two pairs but not the string. Run a few short strings as your own inputs, such as `"abcb"`, `"abcab"` and `"cabcb"`, and check each by hand: `text[start:end]` must have no repeat, and no longer slice may be free of repeats.

KeyError: The usual causes: `last[c]` read before `c` has been seen, or `window.remove(...)` of a character that is not in the set. Read with `last.get(c, -1)` or check `c in last` first. In a set-based window, remove `text[left]` once for each step of `left`.
TypeError: `unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'` comes from `last.get(c) + 1` for a character not seen yet: without a default, `.get` returns `None`. Give it `-1`: one past it is `0`, which can never move `left` forward.
IndexError: A scan that grows a window with `while text[j] not in seen:` runs off the end when the rest of the string has no repeat, as in `"abba"` from index 2. Stop at `j < len(text)` as well.

stopped: In a set-based window, the loop `while c in window:` ends only once the earlier copy of `c` has left the set. Each turn must remove `text[left]` and add one to `left`. Without `left += 1` it removes the same character again: a `KeyError` with `remove`, a loop that never ends with `discard`.

If it stopped on a long input of your own, check that nothing starts over from each position: rescanning from every start is quadratic when the text has many different characters. `left` and `right` should each only ever move forward.
If the run stopped for output, printing the `last` dict or the window on every step is the cause: `test_substring_oracle` runs 1,093 strings. Print two numbers, or only for your own input.
passing: All passing. Try a text with many different characters as your own input: `t = "".join(map(chr, range(20000)))` on one line, then `longest_unique_window(t + t)` on the next. The answer is `(0, 20000)`. Starting over from every position would take hundreds of millions of steps; `left` and `right` moving only forward take 40,000.
